newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Hyder removes uncertainty over UK tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hyder removes uncertainty over UK tax.

text.p: British water and electricity utility Hyder Plc said on Thursday it would pay for its share of a one-off tax on excess profits from borrowings, and ruled out a legal challenge.

Hyder's reponse to the windfall tax, which was detailed in Chancellor Gordon Brown's budget statement last week, prompted expectations that other companies would follow suit to avoid further uncertainty.
"Hyder does not intend to challenge the legality of the windfall tax and it will be paid from borrowings," the company said in a statement.
Hyder said its share of the overall five billion pound tax would be 282 million pounds ($475 million), above most expectations of some 230 million.
It added that it would continue earlier plans to implement customer rebates and maintain its capital expenditure programme, which it had put a question mark over in initial reaction to the budget.
"The market was pleased to see Hyder's situation was not untenable...(but) they have indicated we should reduce expectations on dividend growth," said analyst David Campbell of Greig Middleton.
Hyder said it was "confident that it can deliver satisfactory dividend growth", a statement which one analyst described as "worrying".
Hyder in June raised its year-dividend to 43.9 pence per share from 38.7 pence as it reported pretax profits of 208.2 million pounds, up from 112.9 million pounds.
At the time, finance director Paul Twamley said 11 percent real dividend growth was sustainable but added that it was not a forecast of growth or cover levels.

Shares in the company, relieved of uncertainty over Hyder's plans, spurted 20 pence higher by 1330 GMT to 826 pence, just above its 824 pence close on July 1 but sharply higher than a low since then of 774 pence on July 7 when worries over the tax weighed.
"It has had a substantial risk premium recently and now it's back to pre-budget levels and we think there's some upside," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Hyder's decision not to challenge the tax on legal grounds was seen as a lead for others, with the market hoping companies would prefer to pay and look ahead than risk further uncertainty of potentially extended legal wranglings, analysts said.

There are also concerns that a dispute over the tax, which was a central plank of the manifesto which brought the centre-left Labour government a landslide victory on May 1, would prove politically and publicly unpopular.
The government considers the tax watertight and markets have worried that any challenge might be protracted, costly and ultimately fruitless.
"They're paying the tax and getting it behind them, a legal challenge would bring more uncertainty," said Fraser McLaren of Greig Middleton.

"A challenge would involve a massive amount of work, time and could damage relations with the current government. If one company went for it, there would again be uncertainty and that's ultimately bad for everyone," the analyst said.
The spectre of a legal challenge to the tax was first raised by British Telecommunications before the budget, when expectations were that it might have to pay as much as one billion pounds.
But analysts are intepreting what BT has said since last week's budget as a sign that it will not now launch a legal challenge -- especially as its final bill was 500 million pounds.

Analysts said U.S. companies, which have snapped up seven of the country's 12 regional electricity companies (Recs), might consider a challenge but several are understood to have already made provison for the levy and might be unwilling to ruffle political feathers.
Clarifying the tax has also allowed markets to look ahead and eye possible return of value to shareholders.
"Over the next six months I'm expecting a clear demonstration of shareholder value being released," said Nigel Hawkins of Yamaichi.
Analysts said likely candidates for returning benefits to shareholders included Wessex Water, Severn Trent and Southern Electricity.
Wessex shares have shot up to 464 pence from 434 pence on July 1 while Severn Trent has jumped to 848.5 pence from 810.
"There has been a resurgence of opinion. Share prices across the sector largely reflect the removal of uncertainty," McLaren said. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
